query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (2–3 wt%) of copper during processing will promote the in situ formation of a ductile phase at grain boundaries in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, resulting in enhanced mechanical integrity (i.e., reduced cracking) while largely preserving its high caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric response but poor structural integrity with a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce 2–3 wt% copper into the alloy formulation during melting/alloying to achieve a composite microstructure.
generation.conditions: Under applied magnetic and pressure fields at operational temperatures where the caloric effect is active; mechanical testing via compressive loading in the range of 150–200 MPa.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a finely dispersed, ductile copper phase along grain boundaries that acts to bridge and reinforce the primary caloric-phase matrix.
generation.mechanism: The ductile copper phase, ideally distributed at grain boundaries, will blunt and arrest crack propagation induced by cyclic field and mechanical loading. Its limited volume fraction is chosen to avoid interfering with the lattice dynamics that enable the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in compressive strength by roughly 30–50% with a significant reduction in crack density, while caloric performance remains within approximately 90–100% of that observed in the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits high caloric response but suffers from poor integrity and cracking issues.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under conditions where the caloric response is measured (applied fields and operational temperature ranges typical for caloric operation). Excessive copper addition (greater than about 5 wt%) may begin to dilute the caloric-active phase and undermine performance.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal copper content and its distribution are sensitive to processing conditions; interfacial bonding between the copper phase and matrix must be finely tuned to avoid any adverse effects on the caloric response. The precise numerical improvements are estimated but require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples with identical processing conditions: one set of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with 2–3 wt% copper addition and a control set without copper. Subject both groups to applied-field and pressure-field cycling under the same temperature and mechanical loading conditions.
measurements: Compression testing to quantify compressive strength and crack density
Caloric performance evaluation (e.g., caloric effect magnitude such as temperature/entropy change under field cycling)
Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess the distribution and integrity of the copper phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the copper-added samples do not exhibit at least a 30% improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., higher compressive strength and lower crack density) while maintaining a caloric response within 10% of the untreated alloy. A degradation beyond this threshold in either metric would reject the hypothesis.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs.
